conflict: none — did not build, stage, or assemble
choice_reason: 1. B gives the 60-second decision a single unambiguous primary action ('Reassign to Login') plus per-agent 'Login (recommended)' dropdown defaults; A repeats an identical 'Reassign an agent here' label on all four cards with no default target, so the correct queue depends entirely on the user reading the highlighted card first — the packet's own replayable capture script, which grabs the first enabled reassign button, landed an agent on Billing (lower risk) instead of Login. 2. B announces reassign/undo outcomes through a persistent aria-live=polite region (announce() calls in source); A wires aria-live only to the loading skeleton, so a screen-reader user gets no confirmation a reassignment or undo succeeded. 3. B's 'Needs attention now' hero keeps the single highest-risk queue first in scroll order at both 1440px and 390px; A's equal-weight four-card grid places Login second, after Billing, at both sizes despite the color/badge treatment.
suspected_unblinding: B's source/app.js contains comments referencing named internal process artifacts not present anywhere in A: 'FRAME.md', 'craft.md', 'actions.md', and codes like 'HON-01..HON-06' (e.g. 'see FRAME.md "Candidate elements and deletions" and craft.md's supplied-fact boundary (HON-01..HON-06)'). This reads like a structured internal design methodology/spec used to produce B, with no equivalent trace in A. Not acted on in scoring.

findings.label: A
findings.description: Every queue card has an identically-labeled 'Reassign an agent here' button with no globally recommended/default target. Under the scenario's 60-second budget this creates real risk of allocating an agent to the wrong (lower-risk) queue on a quick first click, rather than the highest-risk Login queue.

findings.label: A
findings.description: No aria-live announcement fires when a reassignment or undo completes — aria-live is wired only to the loading skeleton (app.js line 112), not to the reassign/undo code paths — so a screen-reader user has no non-visual confirmation that a time-critical action succeeded.

findings.label: B
findings.description: The inline error message includes the literal text '(simulated network failure)', leaking internal test/demo language into what should be realistic user-facing error copy.
